title: How the oil market could move from famine to glut | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Wood Mackenzie's Macro Oils team (Alan Gelder, via Simon Flowers' The Edge) argues the oil market is set to swing from Hormuz-driven scarcity to substantial oversupply once a US-Iran peace deal reopens Gulf flows, with Brent falling to US$84/bbl in 2027 and US$55/bbl in 2028 in the Base Case. A lower marginal cost of supply (US$60-65/bbl vs US$70-75/bbl) and ~8 million b/d of OPEC spare capacity point to lower-for-longer prices into the early 2030s, likely forcing OPEC cuts before decade-end.

insights.claim: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz in March 2026 constrained Gulf crude exports and kept Brent above US$100/bbl for much of the following nine months, driving fuel-price spikes, higher inflation and weaker economic growth.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Establishes the supply-shock baseline whose reversal is the core trade: unwind of oil-driven inflation and growth drag once flows resume.
insights.locator: The constraint of Gulf crude exports

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Base Case assumes a US-Iran peace agreement late in 2026 (with no Russia-Ukraine breakthrough), with Strait of Hormuz crude flows normalising progressively through 2027 and fundamentals regaining control of pricing.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: The bearish oil call is conditional on a peace deal; track US-Iran diplomacy as the trigger for the price regime shift.
insights.locator: Why have you lowered your near-term price outlook?

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie expects the oil market to head into substantial oversupply because supply growth in 2027-28 will far outpace a demand rebound, even as Middle East 'legacy' production returns to pre-war levels and beyond.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Positions for a structurally bearish crude curve post-crisis; short-dated backwardation likely to unwind toward contango.
insights.quote: We believe that the oil market is headed towards substantial oversupply.
insights.locator: Why have you lowered your near-term price outlook?

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie added 1 million b/d to its 2027 supply forecast and another 1.8 million b/d in 2028, with just over half of the extra volumes coming from the US (tight oil and gas-related NGLs), the UAE, Brazil and Venezuela.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Non-OPEC and ex-OPEC growth (US, Brazil, Venezuela, UAE) is the driver of the glut — watch upstream producers in these basins for volume growth but price headwinds.
insights.locator: We expect demand to bounce back in 2027

insights.claim: Global observable oil inventories fell by 1 billion barrels in 2026 but Wood Mackenzie expects plentiful supply to rebuild them to pre-war levels of over 7 billion barrels by mid-2028.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Inventory rebuild is a key pathway for the price decline; storage and tanker demand may benefit during the restocking phase.
insights.locator: We expect demand to bounce back in 2027

insights.claim: In its Base Case Wood Mackenzie forecasts Brent averaging US$84/bbl in 2027 and US$55/bbl in 2028.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A ~US$55 Brent in 2028 would be well below many producers' breakevens — a clear bearish marker for oil equities and petro-currencies.
insights.quote: We forecast Brent will track down over the next two years, averaging US$84/bbl in 2027 and US$55/bbl in 2028.
insights.locator: Why have you lowered your near-term price outlook?

insights.claim: In Wood Mackenzie's US-Iran Stand-off scenario, post-midterm US political realignment rules out renewed military conflict, so Iran waits out President Trump's term, Hormuz transits do not fully normalise until after 2028, and Middle East crude output stays ~3 million b/d below the Base Case through 2027-28.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: The alternative path keeps prices elevated for two more years — a key tail for anyone short crude on the peace thesis.
insights.locator: What happens if the crisis doesn’t end this year?

insights.claim: Under the US-Iran Stand-off scenario Brent averages US$105/bbl in 2027 and US$91/bbl in 2028, as non-Middle East supply growth keeps the market long but inventories rebuild more slowly.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: The spread between scenarios (US$84 vs US$105 in 2027) quantifies the value of the peace optionality in oil prices.

insights.claim: Whenever a peace agreement ends the threat to Strait of Hormuz flows — late 2026 or later — the underlying fundamentals mean it could mark a shift in the oil market from famine to glut.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: The bearish thesis is about timing, not direction: the glut arrives whenever peace does.
insights.quote: an agreement ending the threat to flows through the Strait could mark a shift from famine to glut

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie bases its long-term oil price outlook on the marginal cost of the barrel needed to meet demand, and estimates demand growth plus field declines create a 20 million b/d supply gap by 2036 to be filled by reserves growth, new fields and yet-to-find.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Long-term price anchors move with marginal cost estimates; this is the lens for valuing long-cycle upstream projects.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's asset-by-asset data shows more lower-cost barrels available through 2036 (from the UAE, Iran and higher NGLs), cutting the estimated marginal cost of supply to US$60-65/bbl from US$70-75/bbl previously, which could keep prices below prior long-term forecasts into the early 2030s.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A ~US$10/bbl lower long-term anchor compresses NAVs of high-cost upstream assets and favours low-cost producers.
insights.quote: The marginal cost is now nearer US$60-65/bbl compared with US$70-75/bbl previously.
insights.locator: What’s changed is that our asset-by-asset data

insights.claim: Implied OPEC spare capacity stays roughly 8 million b/d through 2036 in Wood Mackenzie's analysis, meaning ample available supply should dampen price upside from geopolitical risk.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Geopolitical risk premia should fade faster than in past cycles; selling geopolitical spikes may be favoured.
insights.locator: Implied OPEC spare capacity remains broadly unchanged

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie expects OPEC will have to cut production before 2030 to avoid a serious oil price crash, with several OPEC members needing Brent above US$80/bbl to balance their budgets.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: OPEC policy is the main upside risk to the bearish price path; watch fiscal stress in high-breakeven members.
insights.quote: We think they will have to before the decade ends if a serious price crash is to be avoided.
insights.locator: Won’t OPEC cut production to support prices?

insights.claim: OPEC+ holding substantial volumes off the market was a material factor in Brent averaging US$90/bbl from 2021 to 2025.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Shows how much prior prices relied on managed supply — removing that support implies large downside.
insights.locator: Won’t OPEC cut production to support prices?

insights.claim: With the UAE now outside OPEC, fewer members remain to share the burden of production cuts, and OPEC may balk at cuts that support prices for recent departees free to raise output — a free-rider problem undermining cohesion.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Raises odds of a market-share war rather than defensive cuts; watch for further OPEC exits and quota discipline.
insights.quote: OPEC may baulk at production cuts that support prices and so help recent departees, which are free to increase production.
insights.locator: The coming years, though, may prove tougher.

insights.claim: Oil and gas companies generated a roughly US$0.75 trillion net cash flow windfall in 2026, much of which Wood Mackenzie expects will go toward strengthening balance sheets to navigate a commodity price downturn, as capital discipline remains the industry mindset.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Expect deleveraging over capex growth; balance-sheet strength becomes the differentiator into a price slump.
insights.locator: How could lower prices affect corporate strategies?

insights.claim: A dip in oil prices could create counter-cyclical M&A opportunities for financially strong oil companies, though buyers may wait while prices stay high, and business development will sharpen toward low-cost, price-resilient assets to offset production declines in the mid-2030s.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Upstream M&A likely to accelerate after prices fall, favouring well-capitalised acquirers of low-cost resource.
